query: For nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and initially crystallized as a solid solution, what governs whether structural and chemical stability is maintained across catalytic and thermoelectric operating ranges of 473–1923 K? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled comparison, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, define the conditions under which the prediction should hold, identify supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Reducing the atomic size mismatch in equiatomic, multi‐metal nanoparticles increases the diffusion activation energy, thereby suppressing the atomic rearrangements (e.g., phase segregation and chemical ordering) that would otherwise degrade the single‐phase solid solution during extended catalytic and thermoelectric operation between 473 and 1923 K.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near‐equal atomic ratios, initially crystallized as a homogeneous single-phase solid solution.
generation.intervention: Systematically substitute one (or a subset) of the constituent metals with an element that has a slightly different (closer) atomic radius to reduce the atomic size mismatch while preserving the equiatomic composition.
generation.conditions: Exposing the modified nanoparticles under catalytic and thermoelectric operating conditions with temperatures spanning 473–1923 K for extended periods, with all other external parameters (e.g., pressure, atmosphere) held constant.
generation.structural_mediator: Atomic diffusion kinetics governed by the diffusion activation energy, which is influenced by atomic size mismatch.
generation.mechanism: Lower atomic size mismatch raises the diffusion barrier, thereby restraining atomic mobility. This reduction in mobility minimizes the onset of phase segregation and chemical reordering, helping the nanoparticles to maintain their initial single-phase structure across the wide temperature range.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles with a reduced atomic size mismatch are expected to exhibit prolonged structural and chemical stability (i.e., maintain the single-phase solid solution) under the operating temperatures, whereas those with higher mismatch will show an earlier onset of phase segregation or chemical ordering.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles with the original equiatomic composition and no intervention, which may begin to undergo diffusion-driven phase changes under high-temperature conditions.
generation.boundary: The prediction assumes that no other external factors (like severe mechanical stress, oxidation, or non-thermal environmental influences) significantly affect the diffusion behavior; the effect is specifically attributed to modulation of atomic size mismatch.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative difference in the rate or threshold temperature of phase segregation is not defined, as additional factors (e.g., variations in mixing enthalpy) may also play a role and the interplay among multiple parameters may induce complex kinetics.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equiatomic multi-metal nanoparticles: one set with a reduced atomic size mismatch (achieved by substituting a metal with one of a closer atomic radius) and a control set with the original mismatch. Subject both sets to identical catalytic and thermoelectric operating conditions, ramping temperatures between 473 and 1923 K for extended exposure durations. Monitor the evolution of microstructure and chemical homogeneity using X-ray diffraction, electron microscopy, and chemical mapping.
measurements: X-ray diffraction to detect new phases or shifts in lattice parameters
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) for identifying nanostructural changes
Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) for assessing elemental segregation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanoparticles with reduced atomic size mismatch do not show a delayed or lower degree of phase segregation and chemical ordering compared to the control samples under identical conditions, then the hypothesis that atomic size mismatch governs the stability would be falsified.

The microstructure of the homogenized NbTaTiV refractory HEA was characterized, using the scanning electron microscopy (SEM) backscattered electron (BSE) technique, as shown in Fig. 1A . A typical simple solid-solution HEA microstructure with grain sizes of 200 to 400 μm was identified without the presence of secondary phases or elemental segregations. decision.trend: Early work on multi‐principal element solid solution alloys focused on how phase structure and secondary phase precipitation were affected by external stimuli such as ion irradiation, mechanical stresses, and moderate thermal treatments. Researchers initially noted that single‐phase alloys (e.g., in Al_xCoCrFeNi or NbTaTiV-based systems) exhibited resistance to precipitate formation, while multiphase systems developed nano‐scale precipitates under irradiation or strain. More recently, studies on quinary refractory high‐entropy alloys produced via advanced processing (e.g., LPBF and magnetron sputtering) have demonstrated that very fine grain sizes and exceptional structural stability can be achieved even at temperatures approaching 2000 K. In parallel, atomistic simulation work has started to reveal that parameters such as atomic size mismatch and the resulting diffusion activation energies are central to controlling dislocation mobility and phase kinetics. However, while these trends offer insights on how high-temperature stability might be maintained in extreme conditions, none have specifically unraveled which mechanistic factors dominate in catalysis and thermoelectric operating regimes.
decision.unsolved: It remains uncertain how the interplay between configurational entropy, atomic size mismatch, and diffusion kinetics precisely governs the onset of phase segregation and chemical ordering (or, conversely, retention of the single‐phase solid solution) during extended exposure to catalytic and thermoelectric operating ranges (473–1923 K). In other words, while evidence points to diffusion dynamics and local strain effects as critical, no study has yet decoupled their contributions to stability under these multifunctional conditions.
decision.lever: Systematic modulation of atomic size mismatch by selectively substituting one metal (or a subset) with an element that has a slightly different atomic radius while maintaining equiatomic ratios and a homogeneous initial solid solution
decision.why: Because the current trend indicates that atomic diffusivity—strongly affected by atomic size differences—is a key factor in dictating the temperature-driven phase evolution, this approach directly tests the hypothesis that reducing atomic size mismatch will raise diffusion barriers, thereby preserving structural and chemical stability across the target operating range. By comparing otherwise identical nanoparticles with varied size mismatches, one can isolate the impact of diffusion kinetics on phase segregation, thus linking mechanistic insights to catalytic/thermoelectric performance cues.
